questions.q: What is the primary difference between Public International Law and Private International Law in terms of the parties they regulate?
questions.a: Public International Law regulates relations between sovereign states and international organisations (e.g., India-Pakistan water treaty). Private International Law (Conflict of Laws) governs disputes between private parties (individuals, companies) with cross-border elements (e.g., Indian company vs US client contract). A wrong answer (e.g., "Public deals with crimes, Private deals with contracts") reveals confusion with domestic law categories — the student is mapping criminal/civil onto international law, missing that both Public and Private International Law can involve contracts, but the *parties* differ (states vs private actors).

questions.q: Explain why the ICJ's advisory opinions are not binding, while its contentious case judgments are binding only on the parties.
questions.a: Advisory opinions (Article 65-68 ICJ Statute) are requested by UN organs for legal guidance — they lack a dispute between consenting parties, so no enforcement mechanism attaches. Contentious judgments bind only the disputing states because ICJ jurisdiction requires *consent* (special agreement, treaty clause, or optional clause declaration). A wrong answer (e.g., "Advisory opinions bind all UN members") reveals the student assumes the ICJ functions like a supreme court with universal compulsory jurisdiction — missing the foundational consent-based architecture of international adjudication.

questions.q: An Indian company enters a joint venture with a German firm. The contract chooses English law and ICC arbitration in Singapore. A dispute arises. Which legal system governs: (a) the contract's validity, (b) the arbitration procedure, (c) the enforcement of the award in India? Identify the relevant Private International Law concept for each.
questions.a: (a) Contract validity: governed by the *proper law of the contract* (chosen by parties — English law here) — concept: **party autonomy** in choice of law. (b) Arbitration procedure: governed by *lex arbitri* (law of the seat — Singapore law) — concept: **seat of arbitration** determines procedural law. (c) Enforcement in India: governed by *Indian law* (Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996, Part II for foreign awards under New York Convention) — concept: **enforcement lex fori**. A wrong answer (e.g., "Indian law applies to all three") reveals the student conflates substantive law, procedural law, and enforcement law — a classic Private International Law error where the three distinct "choice of law" questions are collapsed into one.

questions.q: Compare the 'transformation doctrine' (UK/India) and 'monist doctrine' (US for self-executing treaties) for incorporating international treaties into domestic law. Why does India require Parliamentary legislation under Article 253 even after ratification?
questions.a: Transformation doctrine: treaties do not automatically become domestic law; Parliament must enact implementing legislation (India: Article 253; UK: dualist tradition). Monist doctrine: ratified treaties automatically become part of domestic law (US: self-executing treaties; Netherlands). India requires legislation because Article 253 empowers Parliament to implement *any* treaty, even on State List subjects — this overrides federal distribution of powers. Ratification alone (executive act) cannot alter domestic rights/obligations without legislative sanction. A wrong answer (e.g., "Ratification makes it law in India") reveals the student ignores India's dualist Constitution and the Kesavananda/Magan Bhai line of cases — they're applying a monist assumption to a dualist system.

questions.q: Critically evaluate: "The ICC is a 'court of last resort' — it only prosecutes when national courts are unwilling or unable." Is this complementarity principle a strength or a weakness for global justice?
questions.a: Strength: respects state sovereignty, encourages domestic capacity-building, prevents ICC overload (only 4 situations: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression). Weakness: "unwilling/unable" is politically contested — powerful states shield allies; ICC has no police force, relies on state cooperation for arrests (e.g., al-Bashir case); African states accuse ICC of bias. The principle creates a *gap*: if a state is "able but unwilling" and blocks cooperation, impunity persists. A wrong answer (e.g., "It's perfect because sovereignty is respected") reveals uncritical acceptance — the student fails to see the enforcement-structure mismatch: a criminal court without enforcement power dependent on the very states it may investigate.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical scenario where a customary international law rule conflicts with a bilateral treaty between India and Country X. Apply the *lex specialis* and *lex posterior* principles to resolve the conflict. Explain which principle prevails and why.
questions.a: Scenario: Customary law prohibits use of force except self-defence (Art 2(4) UN Charter + customary). India and Country X sign a 2025 bilateral treaty allowing "pre-emptive cross-border strikes against terrorist camps". Conflict: treaty permits what custom forbids. *Lex specialis*: treaty is specific between two parties; custom is general. *Lex posterior*: treaty (2025) is later than crystallised custom. **Treaty prevails *inter se*** (between parties) under VCLT Article 30/41 — parties can derogate from general custom by special agreement. But *erga omnes* obligations (e.g., prohibition of aggression as *jus cogens*) cannot be contracted out of. A poor answer (e.g., "Custom always wins because it's older") reveals ignorance of treaty supremacy *inter se* and the *jus cogens* exception — the student treats all custom as equal, missing the hierarchy: *jus cogens* > treaty > custom > general principles.
